papers.title: FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals
papers.summary: We introduce a design strategy for neural network macro-architecture based on self-similarity. Repeated application of a simple expansion rule generates deep networks whose structural layouts are precisely truncated fractals. These networks contain interacting subpaths of different lengths, but do not include any pass-through or residual connections; every internal signal is transformed by a filter and nonlinearity before being seen by subsequent layers. In experiments, fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, thereby demonstrating that residual representations may not be fundamental to the success of extremely deep convolutional neural networks. Rather, the key may be the ability to transition, during training, from effectively shallow to deep. We note similarities with student-teacher behavior and develop drop-path, a natural extension of dropout, to regularize co-adaptation of subpaths in fractal architectures. Such regularization allows extraction of high-performance fixed-depth subnetworks. Additionally, fractal networks exhibit an anytime property: shallow subnetworks provide a quick answer, while deeper subnetworks, with higher latency, provide a more accurate answer.

papers.title: Residual Networks of Residual Networks: Multilevel Residual Networks
papers.summary: A residual networks family with hundreds or even thousands of layers dominates major image recognition tasks, but building a network by simply stacking residual blocks inevitably limits its optimization ability. This paper proposes a novel residual network architecture, residual networks of residual networks (RoR), to dig the optimization ability of residual networks. RoR substitutes optimizing residual mapping of residual mapping for optimizing original residual mapping. In particular, RoR adds levelwise shortcut connections upon original residual networks to promote the learning capability of residual networks. More importantly, RoR can be applied to various kinds of residual networks (ResNets, Pre-ResNets, and WRN) and significantly boost their performance. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of RoR, where it achieves the best performance in all residual-network-like structures. Our RoR-3-WRN58-4 + SD models achieve new state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, with the test errors of 3.77%, 19.73%, and 1.59%, respectively. RoR-3 models also achieve state-of-the-art results compared with ResNets on the ImageNet data set.

papers.title: Batch Normalization Biases Deep Residual Networks Towards Shallow Paths
papers.summary: Batch normalization dramatically increases the largest trainable depth of residual networks, and this benefit has been crucial to the empirical success of deep residual networks on a wide range of benchmarks. We show that this key benefit arises because, at initialization, batch normalization downscales the residual branch relative to the skip connection, by a normalizing factor on the order of the square root of the network depth. This ensures that, early in training, the function computed by normalized residual blocks in deep networks is close to the identity function (on average). We use this insight to develop a simple initialization scheme that can train deep residual networks without normalization. We also provide a detailed empirical study of residual networks, which clarifies that, although batch normalized networks can be trained with larger learning rates, this effect is only beneficial in specific compute regimes, and has minimal benefits when the batch size is small.

papers.title: Training Deep Capsule Networks with Residual Connections
Towards Understanding the Importance of Shortcut Connections in Residual Networks
papers.summary: Residual Network (ResNet) is undoubtedly a milestone in deep learning. ResNet is equipped with shortcut connections between layers, and exhibits efficient training using simple first order algorithms. Despite of the great empirical success, the reason behind is far from being well understood. In this paper, we study a two-layer non-overlapping convolutional ResNet. Training such a network requires solving a non-convex optimization problem with a spurious local optimum. We show, however, that gradient descent combined with proper normalization, avoids being trapped by the spurious local optimum, and converges to a global optimum in polynomial time, when the weight of the first layer is initialized at 0, and that of the second layer is initialized arbitrarily in a ball. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.

themes.name: Why skips help optimization: mechanism at initialization
themes.summary: These papers attribute residual benefits to optimization dynamics, not capacity. In normalized deep ResNets, the residual branch is downscaled by about 1/sqrt(depth), which keeps blocks near identity early in training [openalex:W3007689282]. In a two-layer convolutional ResNet, a properly initialized shortcut lets gradient descent avoid a spurious local optimum [arXiv:1909.04653]. Both predict effects that depend on depth and initialization. For a shallow MLP, that suggests any skip benefit should show up as a training-speed or initialization-sensitivity effect, not a capacity effect.

themes.name: Is the identity path necessary? Alternatives and controls
themes.summary: FractalNet matches ResNet accuracy with no identity pass-through, relying on multiple path lengths [arXiv:1605.07648]. This is the closest thing in the set to a control showing the residual form is not fundamental. However, the comparison is not parameter-matched in the sense the author wants, and it is far deeper than an MLP.

themes.name: Adding more shortcuts to deep architectures
themes.summary: These papers add skips to architectures and report gains: multilevel shortcuts in RoR [arXiv:1608.02908] and residual connections in capsule networks [arXiv:2104.07393]. Such additions typically confound the skip with depth, extra parameters (projection shortcuts), and the training schedule. That is exactly the confound the author wants to remove.

paper_notes.contribution: Shows that batch norm's benefit in deep ResNets comes from downscaling the residual branch relative to the skip, by a factor of about sqrt(depth), which biases the network toward shallow, identity-like paths early on. Proposes an initialization (SkipInit-style) that recovers trainability without BN.
paper_notes.limitation: The mechanism scales with depth, so it says little about 2–3-block MLPs where the factor is about 1. It does not examine accuracy differences at small scale or under matched parameter counts.

paper_notes.contribution: The only shallow-depth result in the set. In a two-layer non-overlapping conv ResNet, gradient descent with normalization and a suitable initialization provably avoids a spurious local optimum and reaches the global one in polynomial time. This implies the shortcut changes the optimization landscape, not expressivity.
paper_notes.limitation: Relies on a stylized teacher model, a convolutional (non-MLP) structure, and specific initialization assumptions. Gives no empirical comparison against a capacity-matched plain network on real data.

paper_notes.contribution: Shows that deep networks without any identity/residual connections, but with self-similar multi-length paths, match ResNets on CIFAR and ImageNet. This argues that the residual form itself is not essential.
paper_notes.limitation: Ultra-deep conv nets only. Parameter counts and training budgets are not tightly matched to the ResNet baselines, and there is nothing on shallow or fully connected models.

paper_notes.contribution: Adds level-wise shortcuts on top of ResNets (RoR) and reports improved CIFAR/SVHN error across ResNet variants.
paper_notes.limitation: Gains are confounded with architecture and training changes. There is no parameter-matched no-shortcut ablation, and it is about very deep nets.

paper_notes.contribution: Applies residual connections to make deeper capsule networks trainable.
paper_notes.limitation: No abstract is available, so claims cannot be verified. It concerns capsule architectures and is likely not parameter-controlled; peripheral to the question.

gaps.gap: Two-arm test on sklearn-digits: a 2–3-layer MLP with a residual path versus a no-skip MLP matched on parameter count and optimizer steps, reporting val_top1_err over 20 or more seeds with confidence intervals. Use identity skips with equal widths, so the skip adds zero parameters, and compare against logistic regression at ~3.8%.
gaps.why_open: Every paper here evaluates deep nets or stylized theory. None isolates the skip from capacity and training budget at shallow depth, which is exactly H1.

gaps.gap: Does the residual benefit at shallow depth (if any) vanish when the plain net gets an identity-like initialization or a downscaled final layer? Compare three arms: residual, plain, and plain with a near-identity or zero-init last layer.
gaps.why_open: Two papers locate the benefit in initialization and normalization effects [openalex:W3007689282][arXiv:1909.04653]. If so, a plain net with a matched init should close the gap, but nobody has checked this on a small MLP.

gaps.gap: Separate 'trains faster' from 'generalizes better': track val_top1_err as a function of optimizer steps, comparing the two arms under equal step counts and under early stopping.
gaps.why_open: The mechanisms proposed are about optimization speed and avoiding bad optima, so a difference at a fixed budget may disappear at convergence. None of the papers reports matched-step curves for shallow models.

gaps.gap: Depth sweep (1 to 6 hidden blocks) at fixed total parameters, to find the depth at which the skip starts to matter on digits.
gaps.why_open: The theory predicts a depth-dependent crossover (downscaling of about sqrt(depth)). Where that crossover sits for small MLPs on tiny data is unmeasured, and it would turn a single negative result into a mechanistic one.

gaps.gap: Path-diversity control: a plain MLP with a parallel short and long path (fractal-style join, no identity) versus a residual MLP at equal parameters.
gaps.why_open: [arXiv:1605.07648] claims multiple path lengths, not identity, drive the effect, but only at ultra-depth. No one has tested whether that claim holds at shallow depth.

trends: Explanations of residual benefits have shifted from 'easier residual mapping' toward initialization and normalization effects [openalex:W3007689282][arXiv:1909.04653].
Skepticism that identity skips are fundamental, with path diversity offered as an alternative [arXiv:1605.07648].

Architectural work keeps stacking more shortcuts without capacity-matched ablations [arXiv:1608.02908][arXiv:2104.07393]. This leaves a clean parameter-matched, shallow-regime negative or positive result unclaimed.
The literature concentrates on deep convolutional models. Shallow MLPs on tiny datasets are essentially unstudied in this set.

ideas.title: Pre-registered paired equivalence test: zero-parameter identity skip vs. weight-identical plain MLP on sklearn-digits
ideas.description: This is the grounded version of the author's two-arm idea. Both arms share one architecture: an input projection 64→W (W = hidden = 128), then two hidden blocks f_l(h) = ReLU(Linear_{W→W}(h)), then a 10-way head. The residual arm computes h_{l+1} = h_l + f_l(h_l). The plain arm computes h_{l+1} = f_l(h_l). The identity skip has no weights, so the two arms have exactly the same parameter tensors by construction and need no width compensation. To isolate the path, each seed gives both arms bit-identical initial weights, the same minibatch order and the same number of optimizer steps. The only difference left is the '+ h_l' term. The primary contrast is pre-registered as a TOST equivalence test on the paired difference in final val_top1_err, with margin ±0.5 pp. That makes a null decisive rather than inconclusive. The 'trains differently' confound is handled in two ways. Each arm gets its own lr, picked on an inner split carved from the training data only. As a robustness check, both arms also run at a shared lr grid. Step-resolved validation curves separate speed from final error.
ideas.gap: Open gap 1 (parameter- and step-matched two-arm test at shallow depth, 20+ seeds with CIs), with gap 3 (fixed budget vs. convergence) folded in as a secondary readout.

hypothesis.claim: At two hidden blocks on sklearn-digits, the identity skip makes no practically meaningful difference to final validation error once parameters, initial weights, data order, step count and per-arm lr are matched (H1). Any effect is confined to early-training speed, consistent with the optimization-landscape account in [arXiv:1909.04653] and the depth-scaled shallow-path account in [openalex:W3007689282], which predicts a factor near 1 at this depth.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: The paired mean difference (residual − plain) in final val_top1_err has a 90% CI inside [−0.5, +0.5] pp, so equivalence is declared. Both arms are near or below the 3.8% logistic baseline. At early steps (about 10–20% of the budget) the residual arm may lead by more than 0.5 pp, and that gap closes by the end of training.

ideas.experiment_plan: Architecture edit: add a boolean 'skip' flag to the block forward pass. With depth=2 and hidden=128, the parameter count is identical in both arms; assert this in code. For seeds s = 1..30, initialize the model once from seed s and deep-copy it into both arms. Use the same data-loader generator seed, SGD, and epochs=120 so step counts are equal. Keep weight_decay at 1e-4 and do not vary it, so this stays out of regularization studies. Lr selection: hold out 20% of the training split as an inner validation set. For each arm, pick lr from {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} by mean inner-val error over 5 tuning seeds that are disjoint from s = 1..30. Then retrain on the full training split and score on the official validation split. Robustness: run all 5 lr values for both arms over 10 seeds and report the paired gap per lr. Logging: record val_top1_err every epoch and report (i) final error, (ii) best-over-steps error, and (iii) area under the error curve. Analysis: paired TOST at α = 0.05 with margin 0.5 pp on final error (primary). Secondary: paired bootstrap CIs on best-over-steps error and AUC. Compare both arms against the 3.8 baseline. Cost is about 30×2 + 5×5×2 + 10×5×2 ≈ 210 CPU runs, each a few seconds.
ideas.novelty_rationale: The reviewed papers either study deep conv nets ([arXiv:1608.02908], [arXiv:1605.07648], [openalex:W3007689282]) or stylized two-layer conv theory with no empirical capacity-matched baseline ([arXiv:1909.04653]). None runs a paired comparison with weight-identical initialization, parameters that are exactly matched by construction, a per-arm lr chosen on a disjoint split, and a pre-registered equivalence margin. I cannot rule out that such a test exists in the broader literature; the novelty queries target that.

design.mechanism: The identity skip changes the optimization trajectory: early in training the function stays near the input projection's features, and the loss landscape is better conditioned ([arXiv:1909.04653], [openalex:W3007689282]). It does not change capacity, since the parameter set is identical. At depth 2 the shallow-path downscaling factor is about 1, so the trajectory difference should mainly affect speed, not the endpoint.
design.intervention: Toggle only the '+ h_l' term. Initial weights, data order, steps, weight decay and parameter tensors are held bit-identical per seed. Lr is chosen per arm on a disjoint inner split.
assumptions: Paired seeding (identical init and minibatch order) lowers the variance of the paired difference enough for 30 seeds to resolve a ±0.5 pp equivalence margin on a validation split of about 360 images.
120 epochs is close enough to convergence for both arms that 'final error' means something; this is checked from the curves.
A residual stream without normalization does not blow up at depth 2 with default init. Activation norms are logged to verify this.
design.minimal_test: Run 5 seeds per arm at lr=0.05. Check that parameter counts are equal, that initial weights match exactly, and that both arms train to under about 6% error. Then run the full 30-seed paired TOST.
design.kill_criterion: Two outcomes would go against H1. (a) The paired 90% CI of final error lies entirely below −0.5 pp, meaning the residual arm is clearly better, under both per-arm-tuned lr and at least 4 of 5 shared lr values. (b) The CI straddles the margin, in which case the test is inconclusive and more seeds are needed before any claim is made. If the residual arm is better only at a single lr, the result is attributed to lr sensitivity, not the path.
confound_controls: Parameter count is identical by construction (the skip has no weights), checked by an assertion in code.
Initial weights and minibatch order are bit-identical per seed across arms.
Optimizer steps and epochs are equal.
Lr is selected per arm on an inner split disjoint from the scored validation set, plus a shared-lr robustness sweep.
Weight decay is fixed and not tuned, so no regularization confound is introduced.
design.resource_risk: Low compute (about 210 short CPU runs). The main risk is statistical: validation-set granularity is about 0.28 pp per image, so the margin has to stay at or above 0.5 pp. Without normalization the residual stream could grow; if activations diverge, that is an implementation issue and not evidence.

novelty_review.summary: Judging only from the supplied abstracts, no retrieved paper runs a paired, weight-identical, parameter-matched identity-skip vs plain MLP comparison at shallow depth with a pre-registered equivalence margin. The overlap is mostly at the level of mechanism. FractalNet argues that residuals are not essential. The BN paper gives the shallow-path downscaling account the candidate relies on. The two-layer ResNet theory paper gives an optimization account of shortcuts. The Hourglass MLP paper uses parameter-matched MLP skip designs, but it compares skip placement, not skip versus no skip. This is a provisional difference, not verified novelty. Abstracts may omit relevant ablations, and only one targeted result was retrieved.

comparisons.shared_mechanism: Both ask whether residual pass-through connections are essential to performance, versus training dynamics such as the transition from shallow to deep.
comparisons.difference: FractalNet studies ultra-deep conv nets with alternative multi-path structures on CIFAR and ImageNet. It does not appear to toggle only an identity skip in a weight-identical shallow MLP with paired seeds and an equivalence test.
comparisons.supporting_excerpt: fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks

comparisons.shared_mechanism: The candidate's mechanism is that the skip keeps the early function near identity, and that the downscaling factor depends on depth and is about 1 at depth 2. This comes directly from this paper.
comparisons.difference: The paper concerns batch normalization in deep residual nets and an initialization scheme. It does not compare residual and plain arms at fixed parameters in shallow MLPs.
comparisons.supporting_excerpt: batch normalization downscales the residual branch relative to the skip connection

comparisons.shared_mechanism: Both use an optimization-landscape account: shortcut connections help gradient descent avoid bad optima, which affects the training trajectory rather than capacity.
comparisons.difference: This is a theoretical analysis of a stylized two-layer conv ResNet with special initialization and only supporting numerics. It reports no paired, capacity-matched empirical baseline or equivalence test.
comparisons.supporting_excerpt: we study a two-layer non-overlapping convolutional ResNet

comparisons.shared_mechanism: Both use parameter-matched comparisons of skip-connection designs in MLP blocks.
comparisons.difference: This paper compares where skips are placed (wide-narrow-wide vs narrow-wide-narrow) on generative tasks. It does not compare an identity skip against no skip under identical weights, and it does not use classification error or equivalence testing.
comparisons.supporting_excerpt: maintaining computational efficiency through parameter-matched designs

comparisons.shared_mechanism: Both concern how shortcut connections affect how easily residual networks optimize.
comparisons.difference: RoR adds extra multilevel shortcuts to deep residual conv nets to improve state-of-the-art accuracy. It does not ablate a single skip against a plain network with controls.
comparisons.supporting_excerpt: RoR adds levelwise shortcut connections upon original residual networks

remaining_search: Full-text check of arXiv:1909.04653 numerical experiments, to see whether they include a residual vs no-shortcut comparison with matched initialization.
Full-text check of openalex:W3007689282 empirical study, to see whether it includes shallow-depth residual vs plain ablations.

Broader retrieval on skip vs no-skip ablations in shallow MLPs or small datasets (e.g., MNIST, digits, tabular), including the original ResNet plain-net comparisons and Veit et al. on ensembles of shallow paths.
Search for equivalence testing (TOST) or paired-seed designs in architecture ablation and deep learning reproducibility literature.
Search for work on identical-initialization paired comparisons and on learning-rate tuning fairness in architecture comparisons (e.g., per-arm hyperparameter tuning studies).

papers.title: Rethinking the shape convention of an MLP
papers.summary: Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) conventionally follow a narrow-wide-narrow design where skip connections operate at the input/output dimensions while processing occurs in expanded hidden spaces. We challenge this convention by proposing wide-narrow-wide (Hourglass) MLP blocks where skip connections operate at expanded dimensions while residual computation flows through narrow bottlenecks. This inversion leverages higher-dimensional spaces for incremental refinement while maintaining computational efficiency through parameter-matched designs. Implementing Hourglass MLPs requires an initial projection to lift input signals to expanded dimensions. We propose that this projection can remain fixed at random initialization throughout training, enabling efficient training and inference implementations. We evaluate both architectures on generative tasks over popular image datasets, characterizing performance-parameter Pareto frontiers through systematic architectural search. Results show that Hourglass architectures consistently achieve superior Pareto frontiers compared to conventional designs. As parameter budgets increase, optimal Hourglass configurations favor deeper networks with wider skip connections and narrower bottlenecks-a scaling pattern distinct from conventional MLPs. Our findings suggest reconsidering skip connection placement in modern architectures, with potential applications extending to Transformers and other residual networks.

ideas.steer_link: This acts directly on H1 and the author's request for a two-arm parameter-matched control. It tells the author whether the skip path itself changes final error on digits beyond a ±0.5 pp margin, or only training speed, with capacity, init, data order, steps and lr all removed as explanations.

ideas.title: Pre-registered two-arm equivalence test: zero-parameter identity-skip MLP vs. an exactly parameter-identical plain MLP, with per-arm lr selection and step-resolved error
ideas.description: This idea grounds the author's injected two-arm proposal in the reviewed literature and keeps exactly two arms. Both arms share the same network: a 64->128 linear stem, two hidden blocks of Linear(128,128)+ReLU, and a 128->10 head. The residual arm computes x+f(x) in each block. The plain arm computes f(x). The skip is an identity map between equal widths, so it adds zero trainable parameters, and parameter counts are identical by construction (asserted in code). No width compensation is used. Both arms get the same initialization, optimizer, weight decay, epoch count, batch size and per-seed batch order, so optimizer steps are identical. The 'trains differently' confound is handled with a single declared rule: lr is selected per arm on an inner split disjoint from validation. The full shared-lr curve is also reported so readers can see robustness. The primary contrast is pre-registered as a paired TOST equivalence test on val_top1_err with a ±0.5 pp margin over 30 paired seeds. A null result is therefore decisive and does not depend on the effect being non-zero. Step-resolved validation curves separate 'faster' from 'better'. A cost-free A/A negative control comes from pairing disjoint plain-arm seeds. It calibrates how large a paired difference arises from seed noise alone, so a 'residual effect' cannot be read off pure init or order variance.
ideas.gap: Open gap 1, with the speed-vs-final split from gap 3: no reviewed paper isolates an identity skip from parameter count and training budget at shallow depth on real data.

hypothesis.claim: In a 2-block MLP on sklearn-digits, the identity skip does not change final validation error once trainable parameters, optimizer steps and lr-selection procedure are matched. This is because the depth-dependent mechanisms credited for skip benefits ([openalex:W3007689282] ~1/sqrt(depth) downscaling; [arXiv:1909.04653] escape from spurious optima) are negligible or absent at depth 2.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: The paired mean difference in val_top1_err (residual minus plain) has a 90% CI inside ±0.5 pp at each arm's selected lr. Any residual advantage appears only early in training, in the first ~20% of epochs, and vanishes in best-over-steps error. Both arms land near or below the 3.8% logistic baseline.

ideas.experiment_plan: Edit architecture in the train script by adding a flag skip in {on, off}. Setup: stem Linear(64,hidden=128); depth=2 blocks of Linear(128,128)+ReLU; head Linear(128,10). He init identical for both arms, with the same init seed per paired run. Assert that sum(p.numel()) is equal across arms. Optimizer: SGD with momentum 0.9 and weight_decay=1e-4 (kept at default, not studied). Schedule: cosine over epochs=120, same batch size, and a data-order seed shared within each pair. lr protocol: hold out 20% of the training split as an inner set. For each arm, train 5 seeds at lr in {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} and pick the lr with the lowest mean inner error. Then retrain on the full train split with 30 paired seeds and evaluate on the fixed validation split. Also run both arms at the shared default lr=0.05 and report the whole 5-point lr curve on validation, 5 seeds each, as a robustness view. Logging: val_top1_err every epoch; report final error, best-over-steps error, and the number of epochs to reach 5% error. Primary analysis: paired TOST with ±0.5 pp margin (about 2 validation images), alpha=0.05, plus a bootstrap 95% CI. A/A control: pair plain seeds 1-15 with plain seeds 16-30 using independent init and order seeds, and compute the same paired-difference statistic as a null reference. Compute is about 2x(25+30+10) short MLP runs, which takes minutes on CPU.
ideas.novelty_rationale: The reviewed works test skips only in deep conv nets or stylized theory. RoR [arXiv:1608.02908] adds shortcuts without a parameter-matched ablation. FractalNet [arXiv:1605.07648] removes identity paths but does not match budgets. [openalex:W3007689282] and [arXiv:1909.04653] give mechanisms whose depth or initialization dependence predicts a null at depth 2 but never measure it. We do not claim the comparison is unprecedented outside this review set. The contribution is a pre-registered, exactly matched, equivalence-powered test of H1, with the lr confound handled explicitly.

novelty.closest_title: Batch Normalization Biases Deep Residual Networks Towards Shallow Paths

design.mechanism: At depth 2 the residual branch is not meaningfully downscaled relative to the skip, since the sqrt(depth) factor is about 1 [openalex:W3007689282]. A 64->128->...->10 MLP on digits likely has no spurious-optimum trap of the kind analyzed in [arXiv:1909.04653]. So the identity path should at most alter early-training signal propagation (activation variance roughly doubles across the residual stream) and leave the converged solution's error unchanged.
design.intervention: Toggle an identity skip around each of two equal-width hidden blocks. Everything else is held identical: trainable parameters (by construction), init seed, data order, steps, schedule and weight decay. lr is chosen per arm by the same disjoint inner-split rule.
assumptions: 30 paired seeds give a paired-difference SE small enough (well under 0.25 pp) for a ±0.5 pp TOST to be decisive on a ~360-image validation split.
Per-arm lr selection on an inner split removes the main 'trains differently' confound without leaking validation information.

papers.title: FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals
papers.summary: We introduce a design strategy for neural network macro-architecture based on self-similarity. Repeated application of a simple expansion rule generates deep networks whose structural layouts are precisely truncated fractals. These networks contain interacting subpaths of different lengths, but do not include any pass-through or residual connections; every internal signal is transformed by a filter and nonlinearity before being seen by subsequent layers. In experiments, fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, thereby demonstrating that residual representations may not be fundamental to the success of extremely deep convolutional neural networks. Rather, the key may be the ability to transition, during training, from effectively shallow to deep. We note similarities with student-teacher behavior and develop drop-path, a natural extension of dropout, to regularize co-adaptation of subpaths in fractal architectures. Such regularization allows extraction of high-performance fixed-depth subnetworks. Additionally, fractal networks exhibit an anytime property: shallow subnetworks provide a quick answer, while deeper subnetworks, with higher latency, provide a more accurate answer.

papers.title: Residual Networks of Residual Networks: Multilevel Residual Networks
papers.summary: A residual networks family with hundreds or even thousands of layers dominates major image recognition tasks, but building a network by simply stacking residual blocks inevitably limits its optimization ability. This paper proposes a novel residual network architecture, residual networks of residual networks (RoR), to dig the optimization ability of residual networks. RoR substitutes optimizing residual mapping of residual mapping for optimizing original residual mapping. In particular, RoR adds levelwise shortcut connections upon original residual networks to promote the learning capability of residual networks. More importantly, RoR can be applied to various kinds of residual networks (ResNets, Pre-ResNets, and WRN) and significantly boost their performance. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of RoR, where it achieves the best performance in all residual-network-like structures. Our RoR-3-WRN58-4 + SD models achieve new state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, with the test errors of 3.77%, 19.73%, and 1.59%, respectively. RoR-3 models also achieve state-of-the-art results compared with ResNets on the ImageNet data set.

papers.title: Batch Normalization Biases Deep Residual Networks Towards Shallow Paths
papers.summary: Batch normalization dramatically increases the largest trainable depth of residual networks, and this benefit has been crucial to the empirical success of deep residual networks on a wide range of benchmarks. We show that this key benefit arises because, at initialization, batch normalization downscales the residual branch relative to the skip connection, by a normalizing factor on the order of the square root of the network depth. This ensures that, early in training, the function computed by normalized residual blocks in deep networks is close to the identity function (on average). We use this insight to develop a simple initialization scheme that can train deep residual networks without normalization. We also provide a detailed empirical study of residual networks, which clarifies that, although batch normalized networks can be trained with larger learning rates, this effect is only beneficial in specific compute regimes, and has minimal benefits when the batch size is small.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Importance of Shortcut Connections in Residual Networks
papers.summary: Residual Network (ResNet) is undoubtedly a milestone in deep learning. ResNet is equipped with shortcut connections between layers, and exhibits efficient training using simple first order algorithms. Despite of the great empirical success, the reason behind is far from being well understood. In this paper, we study a two-layer non-overlapping convolutional ResNet. Training such a network requires solving a non-convex optimization problem with a spurious local optimum. We show, however, that gradient descent combined with proper normalization, avoids being trapped by the spurious local optimum, and converges to a global optimum in polynomial time, when the weight of the first layer is initialized at 0, and that of the second layer is initialized arbitrarily in a ball. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.

ideas.description: This is the author's two-arm idea, grounded in the reviewed literature and kept to exactly two arms. ideas.title: Depth dose-response of the exactly-matched skip effect at fixed parameter budget on digits
ideas.description: This idea turns a possible null at depth 2 into a mechanistic result by measuring where the skip starts to matter. For each depth d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}, width W_d is chosen so the total parameter count is about 25k. That budget is the same across depths, and within each depth both arms are identical by construction because the skip has no weights. Each depth runs the same paired two-arm contrast (identity skip vs. plain, identical init, data order and steps, per-arm lr from an inner split). The pre-registered quantity is the slope of the paired gap Δ(d) = err_res − err_plain against depth. The mechanistic prediction comes from [openalex:W3007689282] and [arXiv:1909.04653]: the skip helps by keeping signal and gradients well-propagated early on. So a cheap init-time diagnostic, the input-to-output Jacobian norm ratio (or gradient norm at the first block) between arms, should predict Δ(d) across depths. This is a mechanism test, not a hyperparameter sweep. If Δ tracks the init-time signal-propagation gap, the optimization account is supported. If Δ stays at zero even where propagation diverges, the skip is irrelevant on this task at any depth tested.
ideas.gap: Open gap 4 (depth sweep at fixed total parameters to find the depth at which the skip starts to matter), with gap 3 (speed vs. final error) as a secondary readout.

hypothesis.claim: On sklearn-digits, the exactly-matched skip effect is zero at depth 1–2 and grows with depth. Its size across depths is predicted by the init-time gradient-propagation gap between the plain and residual arms, not by capacity, which is fixed both within and across depths.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Δ(d) is within ±0.5 pp for d ≤ 2 and becomes negative (residual better) by at least 1 pp at d = 6 under per-arm-tuned lr. The regression slope of Δ on depth is below 0 with 95% CI excluding 0. Across depths, the log first-block gradient-norm ratio (plain/residual) at init correlates with Δ at Spearman |ρ| ≥ 0.8 over the 5 depths.

ideas.experiment_plan: Use the depth knob. Set hidden = W_d so that 64·W + d·W² + 10·W (plus biases) ≈ 25k: W ≈ 125 at d=1, about 100 at d=2, 86 at d=3, 76 at d=4, 63 at d=6. Record the exact counts and use the same W for both arms within each depth. At d=1 the skip wraps a single block. For each depth, 20 seeds use paired identical init and data order, with epochs=120 and weight_decay=1e-4 fixed. Per-arm, per-depth lr is chosen from {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on a 20% inner split carved from the training data, using 3 disjoint tuning seeds. At init, log the first-block gradient norm and the input-output Jacobian Frobenius norm on a fixed batch. Log val_top1_err every epoch. Primary analysis: a mixed model of paired Δ on depth with a seed random effect, giving the slope and its CI. Also report a per-depth TOST at ±0.5 pp. Secondary: best-over-steps error and error AUC per depth, and the correlation between the init diagnostic and Δ. Report every arm against the 3.8 baseline. Cost is 5 depths × 2 arms × 20 seeds plus tuning, about 350 short CPU runs.

papers.title: FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals
papers.summary: We introduce a design strategy for neural network macro-architecture based on self-similarity. Repeated application of a simple expansion rule generates deep networks whose structural layouts are precisely truncated fractals. These networks contain interacting subpaths of different lengths, but do not include any pass-through or residual connections; every internal signal is transformed by a filter and nonlinearity before being seen by subsequent layers. In experiments, fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, thereby demonstrating that residual representations may not be fundamental to the success of extremely deep convolutional neural networks. Rather, the key may be the ability to transition, during training, from effectively shallow to deep. We note similarities with student-teacher behavior and develop drop-path, a natural extension of dropout, to regularize co-adaptation of subpaths in fractal architectures. Such regularization allows extraction of high-performance fixed-depth subnetworks. Additionally, fractal networks exhibit an anytime property: shallow subnetworks provide a quick answer, while deeper subnetworks, with higher latency, provide a more accurate answer.

papers.title: Batch Normalization Biases Deep Residual Networks Towards Shallow Paths
papers.summary: Batch normalization dramatically increases the largest trainable depth of residual networks, and this benefit has been crucial to the empirical success of deep residual networks on a wide range of benchmarks. We show that this key benefit arises because, at initialization, batch normalization downscales the residual branch relative to the skip connection, by a normalizing factor on the order of the square root of the network depth. This ensures that, early in training, the function computed by normalized residual blocks in deep networks is close to the identity function (on average). We use this insight to develop a simple initialization scheme that can train deep residual networks without normalization. We also provide a detailed empirical study of residual networks, which clarifies that, although batch normalized networks can be trained with larger learning rates, this effect is only beneficial in specific compute regimes, and has minimal benefits when the batch size is small.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Importance of Shortcut Connections in Residual Networks
papers.summary: Residual Network (ResNet) is undoubtedly a milestone in deep learning. ResNet is equipped with shortcut connections between layers, and exhibits efficient training using simple first order algorithms. Despite of the great empirical success, the reason behind is far from being well understood. In this paper, we study a two-layer non-overlapping convolutional ResNet. Training such a network requires solving a non-convex optimization problem with a spurious local optimum. We show, however, that gradient descent combined with proper normalization, avoids being trapped by the spurious local optimum, and converges to a global optimum in polynomial time, when the weight of the first layer is initialized at 0, and that of the second layer is initialized arbitrarily in a ball. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.

papers.title: Geometric dynamics of signal propagation predict trainability of transformers
papers.summary: We investigate forward signal propagation and gradient back propagation in deep, randomly initialized transformers, and we use our analysis to propose simple and geometrically meaningful criteria for hyperparameter initialization that ensures trainability of deep transformers. Our approach leverages a dynamical perspective in which we regard the token vectors as particles evolving according to the layerwise map of the transformer. We derive simple update equations for the ensemble-averaged geometry of this many-particle configuration starting from a permutation-symmetric simplex. Our analysis reveals an order-chaos phase transition in the forward direction, which corresponds to converging/diverging token angles, and another transition in the backwards direction between exploding/vanishing gradients. We derive the phase boundaries as a function of the initialization hyperparameters, such as the variance of the weights and the strength of attentional and MLP residual branches. We analytically derive two Lyapunov exponents: a token angle exponent that governs the departure from the edge of chaos and a gradient exponent that governs the rate of exponential growth or decay of backpropagated gradients. We show through experiments that the final test loss at the end of training is correlated with these two exponents at the beginning of training, suggesting that simultaneous vanishing of these two exponents constitute simple criteria for achieving minimal test loss.

papers.title: Signal Propagation in Transformers: Theoretical Perspectives and the Role of Rank Collapse
papers.summary: Transformers have achieved remarkable success in several domains, ranging from natural language processing to computer vision. Nevertheless, it has been recently shown that stacking self-attention layers - the distinctive architectural component of Transformers - can result in rank collapse of the tokens' representations at initialization. The question of if and how rank collapse affects training is still largely unanswered, and its investigation is necessary for a more comprehensive understanding of this architecture. In this work, we shed new light on the causes and the effects of this phenomenon. First, we show that rank collapse of the tokens' representations hinders training by causing the gradients of the queries and keys to vanish at initialization. Furthermore, we provide a thorough description of the origin of rank collapse and discuss how to prevent it via an appropriate depth-dependent scaling of the residual branches. Finally, our analysis unveils that specific architectural hyperparameters affect the gradients of queries and values differently, leading to disproportionate gradient norms. This suggests an explanation for the widespread use of adaptive methods for Transformers' optimization.

ideas.title: Where does the skip start to matter? Depth × skip interaction at fixed total parameters with zero-parameter identity skips and a branch/stream variance readout
ideas.description: This transfers the depth-dependent mechanism of [openalex:W3007689282] into a shallow MLP. That paper argues that a skip helps by keeping the residual branch small relative to the identity stream, an effect that scales with depth. Here the residual-vs-plain contrast is measured at depths 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 hidden blocks. At each depth the width is set so total trainable parameters stay at a fixed budget of about 43k. Within a depth, both arms have exactly the same width and parameters, because the identity skip is weight-free. The pre-registered quantity is the depth × skip interaction, not any single contrast. Alongside error, two quantities are logged at initialization and during training: the ratio ||f(h)||/||h|| of branch to stream norm per block, and the first-layer gradient norm. These serve as a mechanistic readout. Under H1 plus the downscaling account, the skip effect should be within ±0.5 pp at depth ≤2–3 and emerge only as depth grows, tracking a collapse of gradient signal in the plain arm. A flat null across all depths would be equally informative. It would mean the skip offers nothing on digits at any depth reachable under this budget.
ideas.gap: Open gap 4: the depth at which the skip begins to matter in small MLPs on tiny data is unmeasured. Locating it turns a single null at depth 2 into a mechanistic result.

hypothesis.claim: The residual advantage at fixed total parameters is depth-dependent. It is negligible at 1–3 blocks and grows at 4–6 blocks. Its magnitude is predicted by the plain arm's loss of first-layer gradient norm and early-training error, not by capacity.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Δ(plain − residual) in final val_top1_err falls within ±0.5 pp for depth ≤3 and exceeds +1 pp at depth 6. The interaction slope is positive with a CI excluding 0. Across depths, Δ correlates positively with the plain/residual ratio of first-layer gradient norm at epoch 1.

ideas.experiment_plan: Architecture edit: an embedding of 64→w, then D blocks of Linear(w,w)+ReLU with `skip∈{identity,none}`, then a w→10 readout. For each D ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}, solve for w so that the parameter count is within 1% of the D=2, w=128 count (about 42.8k); for example D=6 gives w≈78 and D=1 gives w≈190. Both arms use the same w at each D. Shared settings: SGD momentum 0.9, weight_decay=1e-4, 120 epochs, cosine schedule, Kaiming init, identical batch count. LR fairness: per (arm, D), pick lr from {0.02, 0.05, 0.1} on a disjoint inner split of the training data with 3 seeds. Main run: 20 paired seeds per (arm, D), for 200 runs total. Logging: val_top1_err per epoch, per-block ||f(h)||/||h|| at init and at epochs 1, 10 and 120, and first-layer gradient norm per epoch. Analysis: a mixed model of error on depth × skip with seed as a random effect, per-depth TOST at a ±0.5 pp margin, and the correlation of Δ with the gradient-norm ratio. papers.title: Transformers Get Stable: An End-to-End Signal Propagation Theory for Language Models
papers.summary: In spite of their huge success, transformer models remain difficult to scale in depth. In this work, we develop a unified signal propagation theory and provide formulae that govern the moments of the forward and backward signal through the transformer model. Our framework can be used to understand and mitigate vanishing/exploding gradients, rank collapse, and instability associated with high attention scores. We also propose DeepScaleLM, an initialization and scaling scheme that conserves unit output/gradient moments throughout the model, enabling the training of very deep models with 1000 layers. We find that transformer models could be much deeper - our deep models with fewer parameters outperform shallow models in Language Modeling, Speech Translation, and Image Classification, across encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder variants, for both Pre-LN and Post-LN transformers, for multiple datasets and model sizes. These improvements also translate into improved performance on downstream Question Answering tasks and improved robustness for Image Classification.

handoff.topic: Pre-registered paired equivalence test: zero-parameter identity skip vs. weight-identical plain MLP on sklearn-digits
handoff.guidance: Test this idea: At two hidden blocks on sklearn-digits, the identity skip makes no practically meaningful difference to final validation error once parameters, initial weights, data order, step count and per-arm lr are matched (H1). Any effect is confined to early-training speed, consistent with the optimization-landscape account in [arXiv:1909.04653] and the depth-scaled shallow-path account in [openalex:W3007689282], which predicts a factor near 1 at this depth. (expected: The paired mean difference (residual − plain) in final val_top1_err has a 90% CI inside [−0.5, +0.5] pp, so equivalence is declared. Both arms are near or below the 3.8% logistic baseline. At early steps (about 10–20% of the budget) the residual arm may lead by more than 0.5 pp, and that gap closes by the end of training.). Experiment plan: Architecture edit: add a boolean 'skip' flag to the block forward pass. With depth=2 and hidden=128, the parameter count is identical in both arms; assert this in code. For seeds s = 1..30, initialize the model once from seed s and deep-copy it into both arms. Use the same data-loader generator seed, SGD, and epochs=120 so step counts are equal. Keep weight_decay at 1e-4 and do not vary it, so this stays out of regularization studies. Lr selection: hold out 20% of the training split as an inner validation set. For each arm, pick lr from {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} by mean inner-val error over 5 tuning seeds that are disjoint from s = 1..30. Then retrain on the full training split and score on the official validation split. Robustness: run all 5 lr values for both arms over 10 seeds and report the paired gap per lr. Logging: record val_top1_err every epoch and report (i) final error, (ii) best-over-steps error, and (iii) area under the error curve. Analysis: paired TOST at α = 0.05 with margin 0.5 pp on final error (primary). Secondary: paired bootstrap CIs on best-over-steps error and AUC. Compare both arms against the 3.8 baseline. Cost is about 30×2 + 5×5×2 + 10×5×2 ≈ 210 CPU runs, each a few seconds. Mechanism: The identity skip changes the optimization trajectory: early in training the function stays near the input projection's features, and the loss landscape is better conditioned ([arXiv:1909.04653], [openalex:W3007689282]). It does not change capacity, since the parameter set is identical. At depth 2 the shallow-path downscaling factor is about 1, so the trajectory difference should mainly affect speed, not the endpoint.. Intervention: Toggle only the '+ h_l' term. Initial weights, data order, steps, weight decay and parameter tensors are held bit-identical per seed. Lr is chosen per arm on a disjoint inner split.. Minimum discriminating test: Run 5 seeds per arm at lr=0.05. Check that parameter counts are equal, that initial weights match exactly, and that both arms train to under about 6% error. Then run the full 30-seed paired TOST.. Kill criterion: Two outcomes would go against H1. (a) The paired 90% CI of final error lies entirely below −0.5 pp, meaning the residual arm is clearly better, under both per-arm-tuned lr and at least 4 of 5 shared lr values. (b) The CI straddles the margin, in which case the test is inconclusive and more seeds are needed before any claim is made. If the residual arm is better only at a single lr, the result is attributed to lr sensitivity, not the path.. Confound controls: Parameter count is identical by construction (the skip has no weights), checked by an assertion in code.; Initial weights and minibatch order are bit-identical per seed across arms.; Optimizer steps and epochs are equal.; Lr is selected per arm on an inner split disjoint from the scored validation set, plus a shared-lr robustness sweep.; Weight decay is fixed and not tuned, so no regularization confound is introduced..
handoff.lit_context:
Chosen idea: Pre-registered paired equivalence test: zero-parameter identity skip vs. weight-identical plain MLP on sklearn-digits. This is the grounded version of the author's two-arm idea. Both arms share one architecture: an input projection 64→W (W = hidden = 128), then two hidden blocks f_l(h) = ReLU(Linear_{W→W}(h)), then a 10-way head. The residual arm computes h_{l+1} = h_l + f_l(h_l). The plain arm computes h_{l+1} = f_l(h_l). The identity skip has no weights, so the two arms have exactly the same parameter tensors by construction and need no width compensation. To isolate the path, each seed gives both arms bit-identical initial weights, the same minibatch order and the same number of optimizer steps. The only difference left is the '+ h_l' term. The primary contrast is pre-registered as a TOST equivalence test on the paired difference in final val_top1_err, with margin ±0.5 pp. That makes a null decisive rather than inconclusive. The 'trains differently' confound is handled in two ways. Each arm gets its own lr, picked on an inner split carved from the training data only. As a robustness check, both arms also run at a shared lr grid. Step-resolved validation curves separate speed from final error.
Gap it attacks: Open gap 1 (parameter- and step-matched two-arm test at shallow depth, 20+ seeds with CIs), with gap 3 (fixed budget vs. convergence) folded in as a secondary readout.
Supporting papers:
- [arXiv:1909.04653] Towards Understanding the Importance of Shortcut Connections in Residual Networks: The only shallow-depth result in the set. In a two-layer non-overlapping conv ResNet, gradient descent with normalization and a suitable initialization provably avoids a spurious local optimum and reaches the global one in polynomial time. This implies the shortcut changes the optimization landscape, not expressivity.
- [openalex:W3007689282] Batch Normalization Biases Deep Residual Networks Towards Shallow Paths: Shows that batch norm's benefit in deep ResNets comes from downscaling the residual branch relative to the skip, by a factor of about sqrt(depth), which biases the network toward shallow, identity-like paths early on. Proposes an initialization (SkipInit-style) that recovers trainability without BN.
- [arXiv:1605.07648] FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals: Shows that deep networks without any identity/residual connections, but with self-similar multi-length paths, match ResNets on CIFAR and ImageNet. This argues that the residual form itself is not essential.
- [arXiv:1608.02908] Residual Networks of Residual Networks: Multilevel Residual Networks: Adds level-wise shortcuts on top of ResNets (RoR) and reports improved CIFAR/SVHN error across ResNet variants.

papers.title: FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals
papers.summary: We introduce a design strategy for neural network macro-architecture based on self-similarity. Repeated application of a simple expansion rule generates deep networks whose structural layouts are precisely truncated fractals. These networks contain interacting subpaths of different lengths, but do not include any pass-through or residual connections; every internal signal is transformed by a filter and nonlinearity before being seen by subsequent layers. In experiments, fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, thereby demonstrating that residual representations may not be fundamental to the success of extremely deep convolutional neural networks. Rather, the key may be the ability to transition, during training, from effectively shallow to deep. We note similarities with student-teacher behavior and develop drop-path, a natural extension of dropout, to regularize co-adaptation of subpaths in fractal architectures. Such regularization allows extraction of high-performance fixed-depth subnetworks. Additionally, fractal networks exhibit an anytime property: shallow subnetworks provide a quick answer, while deeper subnetworks, with higher latency, provide a more accurate answer.

papers.title: Residual Networks of Residual Networks: Multilevel Residual Networks
papers.summary: A residual networks family with hundreds or even thousands of layers dominates major image recognition tasks, but building a network by simply stacking residual blocks inevitably limits its optimization ability. This paper proposes a novel residual network architecture, residual networks of residual networks (RoR), to dig the optimization ability of residual networks. RoR substitutes optimizing residual mapping of residual mapping for optimizing original residual mapping. In particular, RoR adds levelwise shortcut connections upon original residual networks to promote the learning capability of residual networks. More importantly, RoR can be applied to various kinds of residual networks (ResNets, Pre-ResNets, and WRN) and significantly boost their performance. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of RoR, where it achieves the best performance in all residual-network-like structures. Our RoR-3-WRN58-4 + SD models achieve new state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, with the test errors of 3.77%, 19.73%, and 1.59%, respectively. RoR-3 models also achieve state-of-the-art results compared with ResNets on the ImageNet data set.

papers.title: Batch Normalization Biases Deep Residual Networks Towards Shallow Paths
papers.summary: Batch normalization dramatically increases the largest trainable depth of residual networks, and this benefit has been crucial to the empirical success of deep residual networks on a wide range of benchmarks. We show that this key benefit arises because, at initialization, batch normalization downscales the residual branch relative to the skip connection, by a normalizing factor on the order of the square root of the network depth. This ensures that, early in training, the function computed by normalized residual blocks in deep networks is close to the identity function (on average). We use this insight to develop a simple initialization scheme that can train deep residual networks without normalization. We also provide a detailed empirical study of residual networks, which clarifies that, although batch normalized networks can be trained with larger learning rates, this effect is only beneficial in specific compute regimes, and has minimal benefits when the batch size is small.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Importance of Shortcut Connections in Residual Networks
papers.summary: Residual Network (ResNet) is undoubtedly a milestone in deep learning. ResNet is equipped with shortcut connections between layers, and exhibits efficient training using simple first order algorithms. Despite of the great empirical success, the reason behind is far from being well understood. In this paper, we study a two-layer non-overlapping convolutional ResNet. Training such a network requires solving a non-convex optimization problem with a spurious local optimum. We show, however, that gradient descent combined with proper normalization, avoids being trapped by the spurious local optimum, and converges to a global optimum in polynomial time, when the weight of the first layer is initialized at 0, and that of the second layer is initialized arbitrarily in a ball. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.

papers.title: Rethinking the shape convention of an MLP
papers.summary: Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) conventionally follow a narrow-wide-narrow design where skip connections operate at the input/output dimensions while processing occurs in expanded hidden spaces. We challenge this convention by proposing wide-narrow-wide (Hourglass) MLP blocks where skip connections operate at expanded dimensions while residual computation flows through narrow bottlenecks. This inversion leverages higher-dimensional spaces for incremental refinement while maintaining computational efficiency through parameter-matched designs. Implementing Hourglass MLPs requires an initial projection to lift input signals to expanded dimensions. We propose that this projection can remain fixed at random initialization throughout training, enabling efficient training and inference implementations. We evaluate both architectures on generative tasks over popular image datasets, characterizing performance-parameter Pareto frontiers through systematic architectural search. Results show that Hourglass architectures consistently achieve superior Pareto frontiers compared to conventional designs. As parameter budgets increase, optimal Hourglass configurations favor deeper networks with wider skip connections and narrower bottlenecks-a scaling pattern distinct from conventional MLPs. Our findings suggest reconsidering skip connection placement in modern architectures, with potential applications extending to Transformers and other residual networks.

idea.title: Zero-parameter identity skip vs. exactly matched plain MLP, with a fixed random-orthogonal shortcut as a discriminating control
idea.description: Build 2- and 3-block MLPs on sklearn-digits. Every arm shares the same input projection (64→h), the same h×h hidden blocks and the same classifier head, so the identity skip adds exactly zero parameters. The plain twin is therefore matched on parameter count, FLOPs, optimizer steps, batch order and seed. A third arm swaps the identity skip for a fixed, non-trainable random orthogonal h×h matrix. This arm keeps a parameter-free, norm-preserving linear short path and the same path-length structure, but removes the specific identity map. The design tests the common explanation that the identity pass-through itself is what helps. If any skip benefit appears, the third arm shows whether it comes from identity specifically or from simply having a well-conditioned short linear path, which is the path-diversity reading of [arXiv:1605.07648]. To keep the default lr from favouring one arm, each arm gets its own small lr grid on a held-out split. Final comparison runs over 30 seeds with paired confidence intervals.
idea.gap: Gap 1: a two-arm, parameter- and step-matched test of residual vs. no-skip at shallow depth on sklearn-digits, with ≥20 seeds and CIs. It is extended with a negative control that touches the identity-vs-path-structure question in Gap 5.

hypothesis.claim: At depth 2–3 with exact parameter and step matching, an identity skip does not reduce val_top1_err relative to the plain twin. Any small difference that does appear is reproduced by the fixed orthogonal shortcut, so it is not specific to the identity map.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Paired mean difference (plain − residual) in val_top1_err within ±0.3 percentage points, with a 95% CI that includes 0 at depth 2 and 3. The orthogonal-shortcut arm falls within ±0.3pp of the residual arm. All MLP arms beat the 3.8% logistic baseline.

idea.experiment_plan: Architecture edits: (A) plain MLP: x→Linear(64,h)→ReLU→[Linear(h,h)→ReLU]×(depth−1)→Linear(h,10). (B) residual: same layers, with each hidden block computing z←z+ReLU(Linear(z)). (C) orthogonal shortcut: z←Qz+ReLU(Linear(z)), where Q is a fixed random orthogonal matrix drawn once per seed and registered as a buffer. Verify that parameter counts are identical across A, B and C by asserting sum(p.numel()). Settings: depth∈{2,3}, hidden=128, epochs=120, weight_decay=1e-4 held fixed, same optimizer (SGD with momentum, cosine schedule) and identical batch order per seed. For fairness, each arm×depth gets lr∈{0.02,0.05,0.1}, selected by mean error over 5 tuning seeds on a split carved from the training set. Then run 30 fresh seeds at the chosen lr. Record val_top1_err at end of training and the error-vs-step curve. Report paired differences per seed with bootstrap 95% CIs, and also the min-over-steps error to separate speed effects from final-error effects. Compare against logistic regression at 3.8%. Total cost is about 2 depths × 3 arms × 45 runs, each a few seconds on CPU.

idea.title: SkipInit transfer: does a zero-init branch alone recover any residual gain in a 2-block MLP at exactly matched parameters?
idea.description: Build a 64→h input projection, two h→h hidden blocks (ReLU) and an h→10 head (h=128). Compare three arms that share the same weights, optimizer and step budget. (R) adds an identity skip around each hidden block. Because the widths are equal, the skip adds zero parameters. (P) is the identical plain stack. (P0) is the plain stack with the last linear layer of each hidden block zero-initialized, with an extra learnable scalar gain init 0 on the block output (SkipInit-style, adding 2 scalars). The block then starts as a constant-zero contribution rather than an identity. Notes on P0: without a skip, a zero block output kills downstream signal, so P0 starts at a degenerate function. It still tests whether the init-scale effect, not the path, matters. P0 mirrors (R0), the residual net with SkipInit, which is included as a fourth arm to separate 'skip' from 'skip+init'. All arms are trained with SGD lr=0.05, weight_decay=1e-4, 120 epochs, same batch order per seed, over 30 paired seeds.
idea.gap: Gap 1 (parameter- and step-matched two-arm test at shallow depth) combined with Gap 2 (does an initialization change on the plain net close any residual gap).

hypothesis.claim: At two hidden blocks on sklearn-digits, the identity skip gives no val_top1_err benefit over the exactly parameter-matched plain net. Any small difference that does appear tracks the initialization scale of the branch (R0 vs R, P0 vs P), not the presence of the skip.

Keep the knobs lr=0.05, hidden=128, epochs=120, weight_decay=1e-4. Set depth=2 hidden blocks, plus the input projection and head. Assert that the parameter counts of R and P are identical; R0 and P0 have +2 scalars. Run 4 arms × 30 seeds with a shared seed for data shuffling and weight init per pair. papers.title: Batch Normalization Biases Deep Residual Networks Towards Shallow Paths
papers.summary: Batch normalization dramatically increases the largest trainable depth of residual networks, and this benefit has been crucial to the empirical success of deep residual networks on a wide range of benchmarks. We show that this key benefit arises because, at initialization, batch normalization downscales the residual branch relative to the skip connection, by a normalizing factor on the order of the square root of the network depth. This ensures that, early in training, the function computed by normalized residual blocks in deep networks is close to the identity function (on average). We use this insight to develop a simple initialization scheme that can train deep residual networks without normalization. We also provide a detailed empirical study of residual networks, which clarifies that, although batch normalized networks can be trained with larger learning rates, this effect is only beneficial in specific compute regimes, and has minimal benefits when the batch size is small.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Importance of Shortcut Connections in Residual Networks
papers.summary: Residual Network (ResNet) is undoubtedly a milestone in deep learning. ResNet is equipped with shortcut connections between layers, and exhibits efficient training using simple first order algorithms. Despite of the great empirical success, the reason behind is far from being well understood. In this paper, we study a two-layer non-overlapping convolutional ResNet. Training such a network requires solving a non-convex optimization problem with a spurious local optimum. We show, however, that gradient descent combined with proper normalization, avoids being trapped by the spurious local optimum, and converges to a global optimum in polynomial time, when the weight of the first layer is initialized at 0, and that of the second layer is initialized arbitrarily in a ball. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.

papers.title: Arithmetic-Mean $μ$P for Modern Architectures: A Unified Learning-Rate Scale for CNNs and ResNets
papers.summary: Choosing an appropriate learning rate remains a key challenge in scaling depth of modern deep networks. The classical maximal update parameterization ($μ$P) enforces a fixed per-layer update magnitude, which is well suited to homogeneous multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) but becomes ill-posed in heterogeneous architectures where residual accumulation and convolutions introduce imbalance across layers. We introduce Arithmetic-Mean $μ$P (AM-$μ$P), which constrains not each individual layer but the network-wide average one-step pre-activation second moment to a constant scale. Combined with a residual-aware He fan-in initialization - scaling residual-branch weights by the number of blocks ($\mathrm{Var}[W]=c/(K\cdot \mathrm{fan\text{-}in})$) - AM-$μ$P yields width-robust depth laws that transfer consistently across depths. We prove that, for one- and two-dimensional convolutional networks, the maximal-update learning rate satisfies $η^\star(L)\propto L^{-3/2}$; with zero padding, boundary effects are constant-level as $N\gg k$. For standard residual networks with general conv+MLP blocks, we establish $η^\star(L)=Θ(L^{-3/2})$, with $L$ the minimal depth. Empirical results across a range of depths confirm the $-3/2$ scaling law and enable zero-shot learning-rate transfer, providing a unified and practical LR principle for convolutional and deep residual networks without additional tuning overhead.

papers.title: FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals
papers.summary: We introduce a design strategy for neural network macro-architecture based on self-similarity. Repeated application of a simple expansion rule generates deep networks whose structural layouts are precisely truncated fractals. These networks contain interacting subpaths of different lengths, but do not include any pass-through or residual connections; every internal signal is transformed by a filter and nonlinearity before being seen by subsequent layers. In experiments, fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, thereby demonstrating that residual representations may not be fundamental to the success of extremely deep convolutional neural networks. Rather, the key may be the ability to transition, during training, from effectively shallow to deep. We note similarities with student-teacher behavior and develop drop-path, a natural extension of dropout, to regularize co-adaptation of subpaths in fractal architectures. Such regularization allows extraction of high-performance fixed-depth subnetworks. Additionally, fractal networks exhibit an anytime property: shallow subnetworks provide a quick answer, while deeper subnetworks, with higher latency, provide a more accurate answer.

idea.title: Is it the identity? Fixed random-orthogonal skip vs. identity skip vs. no skip at zero added trainable parameters
idea.description: If a residual path helps a shallow MLP, the cause could be the identity map itself, the mere existence of a short parallel path (the path-diversity account of [arXiv:1605.07648]), or a better-conditioned gradient. papers.summary: This paper presents a supervised hashing framework built on a Siamese architecture, where gated residual connections substantially enhance the quality of compressed representations. The model employs ConvNeXt-Base as the backbone, combining the inductive biases of convolutional networks with modern architectural principles inspired by transformers. In the hash-generation pathway, the learned representation must simultaneously preserve essential identity information and apply nonlinear transformations for effective compression and separation. To achieve this, a learnable gate is introduced between two complementary branches: (1) a shallow identity/residual branch that preserves the core feature structure extracted by the backbone, and (2) a deeper transformed branch that performs nonlinear projection and disentanglement. The adaptive gating mechanism dynamically balances these two paths, enabling the network to retain discriminative local and global cues while suppressing irrelevant variations. As a result, the proposed design produces stable, semantically consistent, and highly discriminative binary hash codes. The Siamese network is trained using Triplet Loss to enforce similarity preservation in Hamming space. Extensive experiments on fine-grained benchmarks (CUB-200-2011 and NABirds) as well as a coarse-grained dataset (CIFAR-10) demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms or matches state-of-the-art hashing methods, validating its robustness and generalization across different levels of semantic granularity.

To match it, F's width h' is reduced, and P's width is set so that P and R also match F's total parameter count within 1%. Drop-path is not used, to keep this out of regularization territory. All arms share the optimizer, lr and step budget. Validation error is logged every epoch, so differences can be read both at matched steps and at the final epoch.

papers.title: FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals
papers.summary: We introduce a design strategy for neural network macro-architecture based on self-similarity. Repeated application of a simple expansion rule generates deep networks whose structural layouts are precisely truncated fractals. These networks contain interacting subpaths of different lengths, but do not include any pass-through or residual connections; every internal signal is transformed by a filter and nonlinearity before being seen by subsequent layers. In experiments, fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, thereby demonstrating that residual representations may not be fundamental to the success of extremely deep convolutional neural networks. Rather, the key may be the ability to transition, during training, from effectively shallow to deep. We note similarities with student-teacher behavior and develop drop-path, a natural extension of dropout, to regularize co-adaptation of subpaths in fractal architectures. Such regularization allows extraction of high-performance fixed-depth subnetworks. Additionally, fractal networks exhibit an anytime property: shallow subnetworks provide a quick answer, while deeper subnetworks, with higher latency, provide a more accurate answer.

papers.title: Residual Networks of Residual Networks: Multilevel Residual Networks
papers.summary: A residual networks family with hundreds or even thousands of layers dominates major image recognition tasks, but building a network by simply stacking residual blocks inevitably limits its optimization ability. This paper proposes a novel residual network architecture, residual networks of residual networks (RoR), to dig the optimization ability of residual networks. RoR substitutes optimizing residual mapping of residual mapping for optimizing original residual mapping. In particular, RoR adds levelwise shortcut connections upon original residual networks to promote the learning capability of residual networks. More importantly, RoR can be applied to various kinds of residual networks (ResNets, Pre-ResNets, and WRN) and significantly boost their performance. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of RoR, where it achieves the best performance in all residual-network-like structures. Our RoR-3-WRN58-4 + SD models achieve new state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, with the test errors of 3.77%, 19.73%, and 1.59%, respectively. RoR-3 models also achieve state-of-the-art results compared with ResNets on the ImageNet data set.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Importance of Shortcut Connections in Residual Networks
papers.summary: Residual Network (ResNet) is undoubtedly a milestone in deep learning. ResNet is equipped with shortcut connections between layers, and exhibits efficient training using simple first order algorithms. Despite of the great empirical success, the reason behind is far from being well understood. In this paper, we study a two-layer non-overlapping convolutional ResNet. Training such a network requires solving a non-convex optimization problem with a spurious local optimum. We show, however, that gradient descent combined with proper normalization, avoids being trapped by the spurious local optimum, and converges to a global optimum in polynomial time, when the weight of the first layer is initialized at 0, and that of the second layer is initialized arbitrarily in a ball. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.
